newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Alusuisse to contribute to Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Alusuisse to contribute to Holocaust fund.

text.p: Swiss industrial group Alusuisse-Lonza Holding AG said on Tuesday it would contribute generously to a Holcaust memorial fund and encouraged the Swiss government to act quickly in joining a fund set up by banks.

"Alusuisse will pay up generously," Hans Jucker, chairman of Alusuisse, told a news conference, adding it is important to remove any tensions that may have arisen between Switzerland and the United States.
On Sunday business executives met with the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti and agreed they were ready to contribute to a humanitarian fund.
Switzerland's three biggest banks, under fire from critics about their role in World War II, have set up 100 million Swiss franc fund for a Holocaust memorial fund.
The banks have been accused by Jewish organisations, Holocaust survivors and their families that they hoarded assets of Holocaust victims placed with the banks for safekeeping during World War II.
Jucker welcomed the creation of the fund and said he hoped the government and the Swiss National Bank would not take too long in deciding whether to pay into the fund.
Jucker did not specify how much Alusuisse would contribute.
The government has said it is working at full speed on the guidelines for a fund it may later join and which will include the bank payment.

The government's position is that it would only decide whether and how much to pay after a panel of international historians presents its first findings on Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre.
Joining other critics of the government's position, Jucker said legal questions really were not the main issue here, but rather "quick humanitarian action that can help in an uncomplicated way."
Alusuisse's German plant in Singen used forced labour from Ukraine during World War II, a fact long known but recently highlighted in a film by Swiss film maker Frederic Gonseth.
Alusuisse's plant in Germany, however, were put under Nazi administration during the war and prisoners of war were forced to work in the factories, Jucker said.
"We are today's generation. We feel morally, but not personally responsible," Jucker said.
Alusuisse's present management took over the company in 1985 and Jucker said very little is known about the company's activities during the war.
However, Alusuisse has made sure historical files have not been destroyed and its archieves are open to historians.
